title: A garden plan
text: Our class had an [[idea]] for a tiny garden beside the library. We chose herbs [[because]] they grow well in small pots, [[so]] even the narrow windowsill could become a green corner.

title: The missing labels
text: The map activity had a [[problem]]: several labels were missing. We decided to [[change]] the legend’s colours after checking the classroom map, [[but]] we kept its familiar shapes so everyone could still follow the route.

title: Water for the plants
text: The chart can [[show]] how much water each plant needs. One clear [[example]] is the mint pot, which needs more than the cactus. That is a useful [[fact]] for the watering team.

title: The class survey
text: One [[reason]] for our survey was to learn which stories students enjoy. The [[result]] surprised us: animal adventures were most popular. We [[also]] found that many readers liked mysteries.

title: A good answer
text: It is [[important]] to read the whole question before writing. A [[true]] answer uses information from the text. If the question asks for a name, that name is the [[answer]]; a long story is not needed.

title: A poster in the hall
text: First, [[describe]] the poster’s colours and shapes. [[For example]], the pale blue background makes the dark title easy to see. One small [[detail]] is the paper boat near the corner. [[However]], the boat may have a larger [[meaning]] because the event is about protecting rivers.

title: The mystery seed
text: The class must [[identify]] which seed grew fastest, then [[compare]] the plants by height. The teacher asks, “What could [[explain]] the difference?” Students should [[list]] possible reasons before choosing one. In a question like this, they may [[suggest|suggest (in a question)]] sunlight or water as an answer.

title: Rainy-day experiment
text: Too little light can [[cause]] a seedling to grow slowly. This can [[affect]] the number of leaves it makes. When the class gives it more light, the leaf count may [[increase]]; if the soil dries out, growth can [[decrease]]. The smaller plant will [[probably]] need more time.

title: A book club choice
text: [[I think]] this mystery, with its clues and unexpected suspects, is a [[useful]] choice for our reading group because it invites discussion. Some students [[agree]] that the ending is fair, while others [[disagree]] because one clue appears very late. Their final [[choice]] is to discuss both views before choosing another book.

title: Planning a field study
text: Before collecting data, the team should [[outline]] its plan and state the study’s [[purpose]]. The aim is to understand how birds use the pond. A clear [[method]] explains how each observation will be recorded. One important [[factor]] is the time of day, because bird activity changes. Photographs can provide [[evidence]] that supports the notes.

title: A careful conclusion
text: The team may [[argue]] that the new sign reduced litter, and the weekly counts [[support]] that claim across several nearby streets. [[Although]] the first week was unusually dry, the pattern continued during rainy weather. [[Therefore]], the change seems meaningful. [[As a result]], the council agrees to keep the signs for another month.

title: Two ways to travel
text: A bicycle has the [[advantage]] of being cheap to use, while a bus can carry more people at once. One [[disadvantage]] of cycling is that rain makes the journey less comfortable. The shelter had a noticeable [[effect]] on waiting times. Adding a second route could [[reduce]] delays, which would be [[significant]] for students arriving before class.

title: Testing a source
text: A [[reliable]] source gives the same key information when checked by another researcher. This is a [[strength]] of the local survey, because many people took part. Its main [[weakness]] is that every response came from one school. The survey was still [[effective]] for learning what that school’s students thought. [[In addition]], the report explains its limits.

title: A story with a message
text: The filmmaker uses colour and music to [[create]] a hopeful mood. These choices [[may]] encourage viewers to help the main character during the most difficult part of the film. A quiet final scene [[might]] suggest that small actions matter. If audiences share the film with friends, that reaction is [[likely]], in the teacher’s view, to [[lead to]] more discussion.

title: Reading a campaign image
text: The first image uses a crowded street, [[whereas]] the second shows a quiet park. This [[contrast]] directs attention to the campaign’s central issue. The calm [[tone]] of the caption shapes the audience’s [[attitude]], although some readers may find the statistics more [[relevant]] to their decision.

title: A review with evidence
text: A strong [[analysis]] explains how a scene creates meaning, rather than simply retelling its events. The reviewer’s [[response]] to the final scene is personal, but examples can make the judgement clearer. The director chooses to [[present]] the young inventor as persistent and thoughtful. That portrayal may [[challenge]] a familiar assumption, while the dialogue helps [[communicate]] the character’s uncertainty.

title: Designing a museum page
text: The page uses bright illustrations to [[appeal to]] younger visitors, while the plain menu helps families find practical information. A moving map on the home screen makes the current exhibition [[stand out]]. Across the floor, short labels [[guide]] visitors from one room to the next. The designer’s [[intention]] is to make exploration feel easy, and the layout may [[suggest|suggest (that)]] that visitors can choose their own route.

title: A balanced review
text: The reviewer notes that science stories [[tend to]] simplify difficult discoveries, especially in short videos. This episode does [[seem to]] give more space to uncertainty. Its careful use of sources is [[convincing]], though one graph alone cannot [[indicate]] how every community is affected. [[On the other hand]], the final interview adds useful local context.

title: The exhibition debate
text: To [[analyse]] the exhibition fairly, students should examine both the objects and the labels that frame them. They can [[discuss]] whether the display gives enough space to different accounts, then [[evaluate]] how effectively it supports its claim. The prompt asks, “[[To what extent]] does the exhibition invite visitors to question its first impression?” A final judgement must [[justify]] its view with specific evidence.

title: A quiet scene
text: From the empty chair and unopened letter, a reader may [[infer]] that the character is waiting for someone. The scene does not [[imply]] exactly who will arrive; its silence leaves room for uncertainty. The grey light helps [[convey]] loneliness, while the close framing seems to [[portray]] the room as smaller than it is. A brief pause can [[emphasise]] what the character cannot say.

title: Whose story is centred?
text: A documentary always reflects a [[perspective]], even when its narration sounds neutral. It may be [[explicit]] about the facts it selects while remaining [[implicit]] about whose experiences are absent. Repeating a single image can [[reinforce]] one interpretation, so editors should [[prioritise]] details that complicate the story as well. That choice does not remove bias, but it can make the framing more visible.
